subject: Stan with small fixed standard deviation

messages.author: f2dbc0d84b28bc86
messages.subject: Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
Hi,

This is a toy 1d example of a model I've been working on where I model the mean with the following function (as written in R) of one parameter (f),

1d_eos<-function(V,f){
  P<-1+(f/(V-0.05))^6
  return(P)
}

with additive Gaussian distributed noise with mean zero and standard deviation sigma. In order to see how stan fits this model I've produced some synthetic data in R, using the true values f=0.1 and sigma=0.0001, as follows,

f.true<-0.1
sigma.true<-0.0001

V<-seq(0.105,2.24,length.out=100)
P<-1d_eos(V,f.true)+rnorm(length(V),0,sigma.true)

I then notice a difference in the results given by stan depending on whether I treat sigma as a parameter, the model for which is,

1d_model_code_sigma_parameter<-'
  data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    vector[N] V;
    vector[N] P;
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=0.12> f;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  model{
    for (n in 1:N) P[n]~normal(1+(f/(V[n]-0.05))^6,sigma);
  }
'

or whether I fix sigma at the true value (0.0001), the model code for which is,

1d_model_code_sigma_fixed<-'
  data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    vector[N] V;
    vector[N] P;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=0.12> f;
  }
  model{
    for (n in 1:N) P[n]~normal(1+(f/(V[n]-0.05))^6,sigma);
  }
'

When I treat sigma as a parameter all of the chains I run seem to converge rapidly to the true value and explore the, very narrow, mode about that true value. When I fix sigma the chains which start with a larger initial value of f (roughly speaking >0.07) converge, but for chains with smaller initial values whilst there is some drift upwards towards the true value of f there is not much movement even running the chains for 10000 iterations. I've attached two traceplots, the first with sigma treated as a parameter, the second with sigma fixed to demonstrate this. I also notice that when I use a much larger true value for sigma, say 0.1, it does not matter whether I fix sigma or not, I seem to get the same results. I'm interested in fixing sigma as when I move to the full higher dimensional problem I intend to use parallel tempering and my implementation of parallel tempering requires sigma to be fixed whilst performing HMC updates, and I use a small value for sigma as this is true to the real data in the application I am working on.

I don't know if there is any obvious reason behind this differing behaviour but any feedback anyone could offer would be welcome.

Thanks,
Michael

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
It may just be an issue with scale during adaptation. It helps
if parameters are on the unit scale (yours for F is about 1/20th of
that), so Stan doesn't have to figure that out during adaptation.

You can look at the gradients for various values of using diagnose
and try to see what the posterior looks like --- it's simple enough
here.

With this declaration:

> real<lower=0,upper=0.12> f;

your initial values for f will be centered
around 0.06. If you just had lower=0, the
draws centered around 1.

You may also want to try putting a softer prior on f
than uniform on an interval. Say something like:

real<lower=0> f;

f ~ normal(0.06, 0.03);

You might want to see what happens without the upper
bound, unless you know there's some kind of physical
constraint.

You can also rescale, so that you take something like

parameters {
real<lower=0> f_raw;
}
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> f;
f <- f_raw / 20.0;
}
model {
f_raw ~ lognormal(0, 2);

You might also try starting with a smaller stepsize and
higher target acceptance rate (adapt_delta).

Finally, you can speed this up significantly
> for (n in 1:N) P[n]~normal(1+(f/(V[n]-0.05))^6,sigma)

by vectorizing the model to

model {
vector[N] mu;
for (n in 1:N)

mu[n] <- 1 + (f / (V[n] - 0.05))^6

P ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

We need to vectorize al of our functions --- we don't have
pow (or ^) vectorized.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
Hi Bob,
I've given your suggestions a go but they doesn't seem to be much improvement. Increasing adapt delta allows 2 or 3 more chains to converge but a significant number continue to drift slowly. I also tried your suggestions about the prior on f, removing the upper bound, and applying a softer prior or rescaling. In each case there still seems to be a region where the chains just drift slowly towards the true value. The attached plot demonstrates this for your suggested rescaling. The model I used for the rescaling (in case I've made an error) is

rescale_code<-'

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    vector[N] V;
    vector[N] P;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  parameters {

real<lower=0> f_raw;
  }
  transformed parameters {
    real<lower=0> f;

f<-f_raw/20;
  }
  model{
    vector[N] mu;
    for (n in 1:N) mu[n] <- 1 + (f/(V[n]-0.05))^6;
    P ~ normal(mu, sigma);
    f_raw ~ lognormal(0,2);
  }
'

One other thing I explored was altering how the model is defined so that the true value of the parameter f is 1, as you mentioned stan prefers parameters on the unit scale. So I rewrote 1+(f/(v-0.05))^6 as 1+f(1/(10v-0.05)) so using the same synthetic data as before f.true=1 for this model. The stan model I used for this is,

rewrite_f_code<-'

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    vector[N] V;
    vector[N] P;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  parameters {

real<lower=0,upper=1.2> f;
  }
  model{
    vector[N] mu;
    for (n in 1:N) mu[n] <- 1 + f*(1/(V[n]-0.05))^6;
    P ~ normal(mu, sigma);
  }
'

In this case I also tried removing the upper bound on the parameter and sing a softer normal prior, but again there seems to be a region of the parameter space where the chains don't converge and just drift slowly.

If you have any further suggestions for what the issue may be or why fixing sigma has such a big impact on the performance of stan they would be most welcome.

Another thing I've noticed is that when I run chains for a large number of iterations to see whether the ones which are drifting eventually converge, if I use the traceplot command with inc_warmup=TRUE after producing the plot my R session reports an error and aborts. This does not occur when I run say 50 chains of 10,000 iterations each but does occur when I run 50 chains of 100,000 iterations. Is there some issue using traceplot on a large number of chains each consisting of a large number of iterations.

Thanks,
Michael

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
Hi,

I've found that for the rewritten model described in my previous post, which is linear in f and where f has true value 1, changing the bounds on the uniform prior seems to affect the adaptation of the NUTS. With my initial prior which was uniform on the interval (0,1.2) I found that, while most chains converge to the true value of f quickly, for chains with an initial parameter value >1.1 they seem to take a much longer time, drifting downwards towards the true value. If you run the NUTS for enough iterations (here 100,000) eventually all the chains make a 'jump' near to the true value, from where they then converge rapidly. The attached file lin_longrun_0_1pt2.png are the traceplots for this. 

But if I widen my prior so that it is uniform on the interval (0,2) I find that all of the chains rapidly converge. There is none of this slow adaptation period in a certain part of the parameter space. lin_longrun_0_2.png is the corresponding traceplot for this prior. The same behaviour holds when I use a uniform prior on the interval (0.8,1.2) as demonstrated by the traceplot, lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt2.png. But again a slight change in the prior so that it is no longer centred on the true value of f, so making it uniform on the interval (0.8,1.4) say (traces plotted in lin_longrun_0pt8_1pt4.png) sees some of the chains which start near to 0.8 take much longer to converge to the true value, when there were no issues in this region of the parameter space with the previous prior. Starting a chain with an initial f value of 0.806 with this slightly expanded prior, and with the seed in stan set to 120591, it takes around 5000 iterations of the NUTS before there is a jump near to the true value. With the prior which is symmetric about the true value however (uniform between 0.8 and 1.2) this initial value and seed sees an almost immediate convergence to the true value.

Bob mentioned in his post how stan likes parameters on a unit scale and how this can affect adaptation and suggested several alterations, and I am wondering what affect my choice of the bounds of my uniform prior are having on the adaptation of the NUTS.

Thanks,
Michael

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
See my comment to this post:

http://andrewgelman.com/2015/10/13/what-do-you-learn-from-p-05-this-example-from-carl-morris-will-blow-your-mind/

What matters is the posterior geometry --- the combination of
prior and data. Changing an interval constraint can do major
things to the prior as shown above. Even if it seems innocuous.

This is just one of the many reasons why we don't like interval
priors other than for parameters constrained to an interval (e.g.,
binomial chance of success parameters or correlation parameters).

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
Remember how constrained parameters are handled in Stan (as clearly
discussed in the manual): the interval (a, b) is mapped to (-infty, infty)
and sampling done on the unconstrained space. So if you put a
uniform prior on (a, b) and expect there to be lots of posterior mass
near either boundary then that can require sampling near one of the
infinities. Stan initializes unconstrained parameters on [-2, 2] by default
so it can take a _long_ time to converge from O(0) to O(infty).

Really we want everything to be unit scale on the unconstrained space.

And stop using uniform priors.

messages.subject: Re: Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
Ok so I should aim to have unconstrained parameters on the unit scale where possible. With this parameter f this is no issue. However there are parameters in my full model which I would like to constrain to be positive, to avoid singularities. I am using the linear model and data above to try to learn a bit more about stan and so have tried constraining this model to learn about the behaviour this leads to.

Firstly I've tried imposing a constraint that f must be greater than 0 and using an exponential prior. The model code for this is,

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    vector[N] V;
    vector[N] P;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  parameters {

real<lower=0> f;
  }
  model{
    vector[N] mu;
    f ~ exponential(1);
    for (n in 1:N) mu[n] <- 1 + f*(1/(10*V[n]-0.5))^6;
    P ~ normal(mu, sigma);
  }
After an initial run I've increased adapt_delta and max_treedepth as prompted by the reported messages from stan and the attached exponentialprior_increasedadaptdelta.png is the resulting traceplot. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
Did you simulate the data you're fitting according to
the model as coded?

The constrained to be positive is better than using square,
which will lead to multimodality as discussed in another recent
post on this list.

When a parameter is positive constrained, it is log transformed
to be unconstrained and it's that unconstrained value that should
be roughly unit scaled for maximal efficiency.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
I think perhaps it would be best if I describe a 1-parameter model with the parameter which I would like to constrain and the results I've gotten attempting to fit this.

So this 1d model has mean (in R)

g_only_model<-function(V,g){
  P<-1+1/((10V-g)^6)

return(P)
}

with additive Gaussian distributed noise with mean zero and standard deviation sigma.

Using these true values for g and sigma,

g_true=0.5
sigma_true=0.0001

I've produced synthetic data from this model in R as follows

V<-seq(0.105,2.24,length.out=100)
P<-simple_eos(V,g.true)+rnorm(length(V),0,sigma.true)

Now previously when fitting this parameter I had used a uniform(0,1) prior, but I know from our previous correspondence that it is best to avoid hard constraints where possible. Now dropping the constraint at 0 is no issue, but the upper bound, at 1, stops singularities appearing in the model and so we wish to keep it. I've done the reparameterisation , g_2=1-g, so that the constraint is g_2>0. Then I understand that the transformation stan applies the log transform to a parameter constrained to be positive. From Bob's previous post in this topic I know that we want parameters to be roughly unit scale in the unconstrained space so I make the further transformation g_3=(exp(1)/0.5)*g_2. Then g_3_true=exp(1) and log(g_3_true)=1, and so g_3 is unit scale in the unconstrained space.

I code my model in terms of g_3 in stan as follows (using an exponential(0.5) prior on g_3),

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    vector[N] V;
    vector[N] P;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
  }
  parameters {

real<lower=0> g_3;
  }
  model{
    vector[N] mu;
    g ~ exponential(0.5);
    for (n in 1:N) mu[n] <- 1 + 1/((10*V[n]-1+(0.5/e())*g_3)^6);
    P ~ normal(mu, sigma);   
  }

Now fitting this model in stan and increasing adapt_delta and max_treedepth as prompted I get the traceplot shown in the attached file g_only_model_pt5.png. You'll note that a significant number of the chains drift towards the true value but do not converge.

Now if I produce synthetic data with a smaller true value of g, say 0.2, and fit the same model, the results are much better every chain converges as shown by g_only_model_pt2.png. Smaller values of g are farther away from the constraint on g_3, so is this an issue with having a true value for the parameter which is nearer the constraint?

Any feedback anyone could offer would be much appreciated.
Thanks,
Michael

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with small fixed standard deviation
parts:
I didn't understand the X axis in that plot --- it's labeled
"chain".

What you want to look at is the curvature (or at least
the derivative). Stan follows the gradient and adapts a step
size to let it move. Often this is problematic when the
curvature varies a lot over the posterior. When you get near
a constraint boundary, the transform can be problematic (for
instance, log(epsilon) as epsilon -> 0).

You said you were keeping the upper-bound constraint on g_3,
but I don't see it --- you just have lower=0. Was that intentional?

- Bob
